summary: Defines how to compute a digest (hash) of an XML document so that the result depends on its content and structure, not on surface differences in how the text is written. Two XML documents that mean the same thing then produce the same hash. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Two people might write the same sentence with different spacing. This gives a way to boil an XML file down to a fingerprint that stays the same even if the spacing or style differs.

questions: why is namespace expansion important in domhash
subtitle: Computing stable cryptographic digests of XML documents.

tldr.problem: Two XML documents can represent the same data but serialize differently, with different whitespace, entity references, or namespace prefixes. This makes digital signatures and change detection unreliable if they operate on the surface string.
tldr.mechanism: DOMHASH defines how to compute a single digest value from the DOM tree itself, not its serialized form. The algorithm hashes each of five node types (Text, ProcessingInstruction, Attr, Element, Document) in a recursive manner, treating namespace prefixes canonically and ignoring comments and DTDs.
tldr.outcome: Two DOM trees with identical content and structure produce the same hash, enabling reliable XML digital signatures and efficient detection of which parts of a large XML document have changed.

today: RFC 2803 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. XML digital signatures are now standardized in W3C specifications like XMLDsig and XML Encryption, which may use DOMHASH or other canonicalization methods. DOMHASH remains valid for applications that need a stable digest of XML content.

sections.title: Why XML Hashing Matters
sections.content:
RFC 2803 defines DOMHASH, a method to compute cryptographic digest (hash) values of XML documents based on their DOM structure. The core problem it solves: the same XML document can be represented as a byte stream in many ways without changing its meaning.

Surface strings can vary due to whitespace treatment, character entity choices (like whether to write & or &), and namespace prefix selection. If a digital signature or change-detection algorithm operates on the surface string, these cosmetic differences cause it to see different documents as having different digests, making signatures fail to validate and change detection unreliable.

DOMHASH takes a different approach: it computes the hash from the DOM tree itself, operating on the internal data structure that represents the document, not on the bytes. This ensures that two DOM structures with identical content and meaning produce the same digest, regardless of how they were originally serialized.
sections.eli5: XML is like a filing cabinet with folders and papers. Two people might organize the papers the same way but write the labels differently. DOMHASH looks at the actual structure, not the labels, so both versions get the same fingerprint.

sections.title: Supported Node Types and Scope
sections.content:
The DOM specifies many node types. DOMHASH operates on five: Text, ProcessingInstruction, Attr (attribute), Element, and Document.

Comment nodes and Document Type nodes are not part of the hash. This is a deliberate choice made because not all XML processors are required to build DOM structures for these; computing hashes this way allows DOMHASH to work with any DOM-conformant or SAX-conformant processor.

Entity reference nodes must be expanded before hashing. Consecutive text nodes without element nodes between them are merged into a single text node; zero-length text nodes are ignored. The hash values are defined recursively: each parent node's hash incorporates the hashes of its children, so if a small part of a large tree changes, only the relevant hashes need recalculation.
sections.eli5: The hash ignores comments and type declarations because not every XML reader understands those. It treats a long run of text as one piece, even if it was stored in chunks, and it builds the hash from the inside out so small changes are cheap to recompute.

sections.title: Computing Digests for Each Node Type
sections.content:
Each node type produces a digest in a specific format, using a standard hash algorithm like MD5 or SHA-1. All strings are encoded as UTF-16BE (big-endian).

Text nodes are hashed as a 4-byte node-type header (value 3) followed by the UTF-16BE encoded text.

ProcessingInstruction nodes are hashed as a header (value 7) followed by the target, a two-byte separator (0x0000), and the data, all in UTF-16BE.

Attr nodes use the expanded name of the attribute (with namespace prefix resolved), a 4-byte header (value 2), the expanded name in UTF-16BE, a two-byte separator, and the attribute value. Namespace declarations themselves (attributes named 'xmlns' or with prefix 'xmlns') produce no digest.

Element nodes (the most complex) include the node-type header (value 1), the expanded element name, a separator, a count of non-namespace attributes sorted lexicographically by expanded name, the digests of those attributes, a count of child nodes, and the digests of child nodes in order.

Document nodes are hashed as a header (value 9), a count of children (excluding comments and DocumentType nodes), and the digests of those children in order.
sections.eli5: Each type of node gets a number and a digest recipe. Text is just text. Attributes are name plus value. Elements bundle their attributes and children. The algorithm computes from the bottom up: leaves first, then parents.

sections.title: Security and Namespace Normalization
sections.content:
A critical challenge in XML is namespace handling. Different namespace prefixes can represent the same namespace URI, yet both are valid and mean the same thing. DOMHASH solves this by using expanded names: a qualified element or attribute name is replaced with the namespace URI plus a colon plus the local part. Namespace declaration attributes themselves are excluded from the digest because they are only markup, not content.

Regarding security, DOMHASH is intended as a basis for digital signatures and integrity checks. Its suitability for such uses depends on the strength of the underlying hash algorithm. When using DOMHASH to sign data, the original sender should sign the actual serialized bytes of the document, then verify that the signed data, when parsed and hashed with DOMHASH, matches a reference digest. Note that stripping a leading 0xFEFF byte order mark before hashing can affect external processes like digital signature verification.
sections.eli5: Namespace prefixes are just labels. DOMHASH uses the actual namespace (the real name), not the label, so 'edi:order' and 'ec:order' pointing to the same namespace get the same digest. When signing, always sign the actual bytes, not just the digest.
